summary: This document expands, updates, and establishes an IANA registry for the URIs used with XML digital signatures, encryption, canonicalization, and key management. The URIs identify algorithms and types of information. It obsoletes RFC 4051 and was itself replaced by RFC 9231.

eli5.summary: XML security uses web-address-style labels to say which method was used. This is the official list of those labels. A newer list has since replaced it.

subtitle: The official registry of algorithm identifiers for XML security.

tldr.problem: XML security standards (signatures, encryption, key management, and canonicalization) reference cryptographic algorithms by URI identifiers, but the list was incomplete and outdated as new algorithms emerged.
tldr.mechanism: This document expands and consolidates the registry of URIs used to identify algorithms in XML security specifications, providing identifiers for hash functions, signature algorithms, encryption methods, and key information types.
tldr.outcome: A comprehensive, maintainable list of algorithm identifiers that allow implementers to correctly specify which cryptographic methods are in use. RFC 9231 provides the current registry.

facts.label: Standards referenced
facts.value: XML Signature 1.0/1.1, XML Encryption 1.0/1.1, Canonical XML

today: RFC 6931 is a Proposed Standard. It was superseded by RFC 9231 in October 2022, which continues to maintain the IANA registry of algorithm URIs. For current algorithm identifiers in XML security applications, RFC 9231 should be used.

sections.title: XML Security and Algorithm Identification
sections.content:
The W3C and IETF standardized a family of specifications for securing XML documents: XML Digital Signatures, XML Encryption, canonical XML (a standardized way to represent XML), and key management techniques. These specifications are published as W3C Recommendations and Internet RFCs.

All these specifications use Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) to identify which cryptographic algorithm is being used. For example, instead of writing 'use SHA-256' as a string, a specification might use the URI http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmldsig-more#sha256. This approach allows for unambiguous, globally unique identification of algorithms across different systems and specifications.

RFC 4051, published in 2005, first compiled a comprehensive list of these algorithm URIs. However, by the time this document was written, new cryptographic algorithms (such as SHA-3, Camellia, and SEED) and updated XML security standards (XML Signature 1.1 and XML Encryption 1.1) had introduced additional algorithms. This RFC expands RFC 4051 with these new identifiers and maintains a centralized registry.
sections.eli5: When you sign or encrypt something in XML, you need to say which math method you used. This document is the official list of web-address-style labels for those methods, so everyone knows what you mean.

sections.title: Algorithm Categories
sections.content:
The RFC organizes algorithm URIs into several categories. Digest method (hash) algorithms include SHA-224, SHA-384, Whirlpool, and SHA-3 variants. These are used to create a fixed-size fingerprint of data for integrity checking.

Signature method MAC algorithms include HMAC-MD5, HMAC-SHA variants, and HMAC-RIPEMD160. These combine a secret key with a hash function to create a message authentication code, proving both integrity and authenticity when both parties share a secret key.

Public-key signature algorithms use asymmetric cryptography where the signing and verification keys are different. These include RSA-based methods (RSA-MD5, RSA-SHA256, RSA-SHA384, RSA-SHA512, RSA-RIPEMD160, RSA-Whirlpool), ECDSA variants (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm combined with various hash functions), ESIGN (a signature scheme based on integer factorization), and RSASSA-PSS with various parameters.

Canonicalization algorithms standardize the representation of XML to ensure consistent hashing across different XML parsers and formatting. The RFC includes minimal canonicalization and references to other canonicalization methods.

Encryption algorithms include ARCFOUR (a stream cipher), Camellia block encryption in various key sizes, SEED block encryption, and PSEC-KEM (a key encapsulation mechanism using elliptic curves).
sections.eli5: The document lists web-address labels for different types of math operations: hashing (fingerprinting), signing with a shared secret, signing with a private key, organizing XML data, and encrypting data.

sections.title: URI Namespaces and Organization
sections.content:
Algorithm URIs are organized under several W3C namespaces. The base XML Digital Signature namespace (http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#) contains the original algorithms from the XML Digital Signature specification. Algorithms added in RFC 4051 use the namespace (http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmldsig-more#). New algorithms in this document are given URIs in the namespace (http://www.w3.org/2007/05/xmldsig-more#).

Similarly, XML Encryption algorithms use namespaces like http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmlenc# and the updated namespace http://www.w3.org/2009/xmlenc11#.

The organization by namespace allows new algorithms to be added without conflicts and provides a clear history of when each algorithm was registered. The RFC provides comprehensive indexes organized by fragment identifier (the part after '#') and by full URI for easy lookup.
sections.eli5: The labels are grouped into collections based on when they were added. This helps organize the list and avoids name conflicts when new algorithms are invented.

sections.title: Key Information and Additional Elements
sections.content:
Beyond algorithms, XML security specifications need ways to represent key information. The RFC defines URIs for PKCS #7 bags of certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs), allowing X.509 certificate chains to be embedded in XML using standard PKCS #7 encoding.

Additional RetrievalMethod type values are defined to identify different key information types when retrieving keys from external sources: KeyName (a named key), KeyValue (key material), PKCS7signedData, raw PGP key packets, raw PKCS #7 structures, raw SPKI S-expressions, and raw X.509 CRLs.

These identifiers allow specifications to unambiguously state what type of key information is present and how to interpret and extract the actual key material.
sections.eli5: The document also includes labels for different ways to store keys and certificates in XML, so readers know exactly how to interpret the data.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Maintenance
sections.content:
The RFC establishes an IANA registry for XML security URIs, providing a mechanism for new algorithms to be registered in the future. The registry is maintained by IANA with oversight by the W3C and IETF, allowing the list to grow as new cryptographic standards emerge.

The document includes comprehensive indexes organized in two ways: by fragment identifier (the short name after '#') and by full URI. These indexes make it easy to look up an algorithm or find its identifier. The indexes also note which document defines each algorithm (this RFC, RFC 3275 for original XML Digital Signatures, RFC 3741 for exclusive canonicalization, etc.).

Because cryptographic algorithms and standards constantly evolve, the registry approach allows the list to be extended through subsequent documents without requiring updates to the core XML security specifications.
sections.eli5: This creates an official list that can be updated over time as new encryption methods are invented, without changing the core XML security standards themselves.

sections.title: Document Status and Supersession
sections.content: RFC 6931 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4051 from 2005. It consolidates and updates the algorithm registry with new cryptographic methods and updated XML security specifications that emerged in the intervening years. The document was itself superseded by RFC 9231 in October 2022, which provides further updates and additions to the algorithm registry.
sections.eli5: This RFC updated an earlier list from 2005. A newer version (RFC 9231) came out in 2022 with additional algorithms. Use RFC 9231 for the current list.
